subtopic_detail: Distinguishing structural clubfoot from positional foot deformity in the newborn and the timing of Ponseti casting
stem:
You are the resident reviewing a 3-day-old boy on the postnatal ward before discharge. His mother says both of his feet 'turn in and point down' and that they have looked this way since birth.

He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy with normal liquor volume. Birth weight was 3300 g and he is feeding well.

On examination both forefeet are adducted and both heels are held in varus and equinus. Neither foot can be brought up past 20 degrees of plantarflexion despite firm pressure, and there is a deep transverse crease across each medial arch. Both calves are visibly thinner than expected for his size. Hip abduction is full and symmetrical with no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral forefoot adduction with hindfoot varus and equinus; neither foot correctable past 20 degrees of plantarflexion
data_table.Skin and soft tissue: Deep transverse medial arch crease bilaterally; bilateral calf wasting
data_table.Hips: Full symmetrical abduction, Ortolani and Barlow negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for Ponseti serial casting to start this week
options.rationale: Rigid equinovarus that will not correct past plantarflexion, with a deep medial crease and calf wasting, is structural talipes equinovarus rather than a positional deformity. Ponseti casting is most effective when started in the first weeks of life while the ligaments are still highly responsive to maternal relaxin, so referral is made before discharge rather than deferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Teach the parents passive stretching exercises and review the feet at six weeks
options.rationale: Passive stretching is the treatment for positional talipes, which is soft and fully correctable to a neutral dorsiflexed position at the cot side. These feet are fixed in equinus with skin creases and calf wasting, and six weeks of stretching would waste the window in which casting works best. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Arrange a foot and ankle ultrasound before deciding on orthopaedic referral
options.rationale: Talipes equinovarus is a clinical diagnosis made on rigidity and the classic crease and calf findings, and imaging of the foot does not change the decision to cast. Imaging is reserved for atypical or syndromic feet being planned for surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Apply overnight below-knee splints and refer to orthopaedics at three months
options.rationale: Bracing has a role only after the deformity has been corrected by casting, as the Ponseti maintenance phase with a foot abduction orthosis. Splinting an uncorrected rigid foot achieves nothing and a three month delay materially worsens the number of casts needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound at six weeks and refer if the feet remain deformed
options.rationale: Hip imaging is the right reflex when a foot deformity coexists with risk factors or an abnormal hip examination, but abduction here is full and symmetrical with negative Ortolani and Barlow testing. Deferring the foot referral to the hip scan appointment delays the time-critical intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Foot deformity in the newborn splits into positional deformity, which is supple and self-correcting, and structural talipes equinovarus, which is rigid and needs treatment. The three findings that mark the structural form are failure to correct the equinus passively, deep medial and posterior skin creases, and wasting of the calf, all of which reflect a genuinely short and abnormal posteromedial soft tissue complex. The Ponseti method uses weekly manipulation and above-knee casting, usually followed by a percutaneous tendo-Achilles tenotomy, and then a foot abduction orthosis worn for several years. Treatment started in the first weeks of life needs fewer casts and achieves better long-term function than treatment deferred to later infancy. Untreated clubfoot leads to weight bearing on the lateral border of the foot with callus, pain and disability.
key_points: Rigidity, creases and calf wasting separate structural talipes from positional deformity
Ponseti casting should begin in the first weeks of life, not after a period of observation
Imaging of the foot does not guide the decision to cast
Bracing belongs to the maintenance phase after casting has corrected the deformity
Examine the hips in every infant with a foot deformity, but a normal hip examination does not delay foot referral
explanation.pearls: The Ponseti maintenance orthosis is worn 23 hours a day for the first 3 months after casting and then at night until about age 4; non-adherence to the brace is the single largest driver of recurrence.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
BMJ Best Practice: Congenital talipes equinovarus

subtopic_detail: Minimum interval between two parenteral live vaccines when catching up an incompletely vaccinated child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15-month-old girl who arrived in Australia six weeks ago. Her mother brings a handwritten card from their previous country listing three doses of a diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis containing vaccine and two doses of polio vaccine, with no record of any measles containing vaccine.

Ten days ago the family attended a different practice, where she was given a measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. The mother now wants 'everything else she has missed' done today so the child can start childcare.

The girl is well, afebrile and thriving, with no immunosuppressive conditions and no medications. She has had no blood products or immunoglobulin. You determine that she still requires varicella vaccine and a Haemophilus influenzae type b containing vaccine.

data_table.Vaccines documented: Three doses diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine, two doses polio vaccine
data_table.Recent vaccine: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine given 10 days ago at another practice
data_table.Still required today: Varicella vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b containing vaccine
data_table.Examination: Well and afebrile, growth on the 50th centile, no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for the varicella vaccine?

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine today at a separate injection site
options.rationale: Two parenteral live vaccines must be given either on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart, and 10 days falls inside that window. Giving it today risks interferon mediated blunting of the varicella response, which would then require a repeat dose. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine at least four weeks after the measles vaccine
options.rationale: Where two parenteral live vaccines are not given on the same day, the minimum interval is 4 weeks, so the varicella dose is scheduled for at least 28 days after the measles containing vaccine. The Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine is inactivated and can be given today without waiting. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Check varicella and measles serology first and vaccinate only if she is not immune
options.rationale: Serological testing is not required before catch-up vaccination in a well child with no documented disease, and vaccinating a person who is already immune is safe. Pre-vaccination serology is reserved for specific groups such as some hepatitis B and varicella exposures in adults. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Administer the varicella vaccine one week from now with paracetamol cover
options.rationale: One week still falls short of the 4 week minimum interval between two parenteral live vaccines. Routine prophylactic paracetamol is also not recommended because it can reduce antibody responses and is reserved for specific meningococcal B schedules. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Repeat the measles vaccine today and give the varicella vaccine in three months
options.rationale: The measles containing dose 10 days ago was valid and counts towards her schedule, so repeating it adds no benefit. Three months is the interval used after an immunoglobulin or blood product exposure, which she has not had. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Catch-up schedules turn on a small number of interval rules rather than on the individual vaccine. Inactivated vaccines can be co-administered with anything and have no minimum spacing from other vaccines, so the Haemophilus influenzae type b dose proceeds today. Two parenteral live vaccines interact through a transient interferon response, so they are given on the same day or separated by at least 4 weeks; if the interval is breached the second dose is invalid and must be repeated. Live oral vaccines such as rotavirus are exempt from this rule. Children under 10 years presenting for catch-up can complete a full schedule relatively quickly because most remaining antigens are inactivated.
key_points: Two parenteral live vaccines: same day, or at least 4 weeks apart
A dose given inside the 4 week window is invalid and must be repeated
Inactivated vaccines have no minimum interval from other vaccines
Pre-vaccination serology is not routine in catch-up of a well child
Live oral vaccines are not subject to the 4 week parenteral live vaccine rule
explanation.pearls: Tuberculin skin testing is suppressed by measles containing vaccine: do the skin test on the same day as the vaccine or wait at least 4 weeks, otherwise a false negative is likely.

subtopic_detail: Choice of scabicide in an infant below the minimum age for topical permethrin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 6-week-old boy whose mother says he has become 'covered in angry spots' over the past fortnight and cries and squirms most of the night.

He was born at term and is breastfed and thriving. His mother has had an intensely itchy rash on her wrists and between her fingers for about six weeks, and his 4-year-old sister has a similar itchy rash.

On examination there are erythematous papules and pustules scattered over the trunk, and vesicles and burrows involving both palms and both soles as well as the scalp. Skin scrapings taken in clinic show a mite and several ova on light microscopy.

data_table.Examination: Papules and pustules on trunk; vesicles and burrows on palms, soles and scalp
data_table.Investigations: Skin scraping microscopy shows a mite and ova
data_table.Household: Mother and 4-year-old sister both have an itchy rash of about six weeks duration
data_table.Growth and feeding: Exclusively breastfed, weight tracking on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Apply permethrin 5 per cent cream to the infant and treat all household contacts
options.rationale: Permethrin 5 per cent is the standard Australian first-line scabicide but is not recommended below 2 months of age, and this infant is 6 weeks old. It is the right agent for the mother and sister, who should be treated on the same day. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

options.text: Apply benzyl benzoate 25 per cent lotion to the infant and all household contacts
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is highly irritant on infant skin and at full strength risks a severe chemical dermatitis, so it is not used in this age group. It is a second-line agent for older children and adults when permethrin has failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply sulfur 5 per cent ointment to the infant and treat all household contacts
options.rationale: Sulfur in white soft paraffin is the preferred scabicide below 2 months of age, applied to the whole body including scalp, face, palms and soles for three consecutive nights. Simultaneous treatment of every household member on the same day is what prevents the cycle of reinfestation from the untreated mother and sister. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral ivermectin to the infant and all household contacts
options.rationale: Oral ivermectin is not used under 15 kg because safety data in small infants are lacking, and it is reserved for crusted scabies, outbreaks or treatment failure. It would be a reasonable adjunct for adult contacts in a crusted scabies scenario, which this is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply hydrocortisone 1 per cent to the infant and treat the contacts with permethrin
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats the eczematous reaction but leaves the mite alive, and used alone it can produce the poorly inflamed, widely disseminated picture of scabies incognito. Steroid has a place only alongside a scabicide for persistent post-scabetic itch. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

explanation.summary: Scabies in infants differs from the adult disease in both distribution and treatment. Infants characteristically involve the scalp, face, palms and soles, sites that are deliberately spared when treating adults, so the application instructions change with age. Permethrin 5 per cent is the Australian first-line agent from 2 months onward, and sulfur preparations fill the gap below that age. Treatment fails far more often because contacts were not treated simultaneously than because the drug was wrong, so every household member and any regular carer is treated on the same day regardless of symptoms. Itch persists for 2 to 4 weeks after successful treatment and is not by itself evidence of failure.
key_points: Permethrin 5 per cent is first line from 2 months of age; below that use sulfur in white soft paraffin
In infants apply the scabicide to scalp, face, palms and soles as well as the body
Treat every household member on the same day, symptomatic or not
Oral ivermectin is avoided under 15 kg and is reserved for crusted scabies or failure
Post-scabetic itch lasting 2 to 4 weeks does not mean treatment failed
explanation.pearls: Wash bedding and clothing in hot water on the day of treatment; items that cannot be washed are sealed in a plastic bag for 72 hours, which exceeds the time a mite survives off human skin.

subtopic_detail: Management of cyanotic breath-holding spells when iron studies are abnormal
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric assessment unit reviewing an 18-month-old boy brought in after an episode at home. His mother says he was told he could not have a biscuit, cried hard for about fifteen seconds, then 'went silent, turned blue around the lips and flopped'. He was limp for roughly ten seconds, then took a breath and was crying and reaching for her within half a minute.

There have been six such episodes in four months, every one of them beginning with a period of prolonged crying after frustration or a minor injury. He has never had an episode during sleep, at rest or during exercise, and there has been no jerking of the limbs and no incontinence.

He is developmentally normal and drinks about a litre of cow milk daily. Cardiovascular examination is normal with equal volume femoral pulses. Blood tests are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 120/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 68 fL (73-85), ferritin 7 microgram/L (15-150), electrolytes and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal tone and development, normal heart sounds, equal volume femoral pulses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram before starting any specific treatment
options.rationale: Every episode has been preceded by a prolonged cry with an identifiable provocation, which is the hallmark of a breath-holding spell rather than a seizure. Electroencephalography would be indicated if events occurred without a trigger, during sleep, or with a prolonged postictal phase, none of which applies here. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for an echocardiogram and exercise testing
options.rationale: Structural heart disease is suggested by events at rest or on exertion, a murmur or abnormal pulses, and cardiovascular examination and femoral pulses are normal. Echocardiography is the wrong test for a child whose episodes are reliably provoked by crying. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Commence oral sodium valproate and review the frequency of episodes in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antiseizure medication has no role in breath-holding spells because the events are reflex in origin rather than epileptic. Valproate would additionally be a poor first choice in any young child given its hepatic and metabolic risks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence oral iron supplementation and review the frequency of episodes in eight weeks
options.rationale: Microcytic anaemia with a ferritin of 7 microgram/L confirms iron deficiency, driven here by an intake of about a litre of cow milk daily, and treating it reduces both the frequency and severity of breath-holding spells. Iron is given for at least 3 months to refill stores, with parental reassurance about the benign natural history and first aid positioning. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

options.text: Arrange a 12 lead electrocardiogram and withhold treatment until the result is available
options.rationale: An electrocardiogram is a reasonable screen when spells are of the pallid type, occur without a preceding cry, or there is a family history of sudden death, and it can be done in parallel rather than as a reason to withhold iron. Here the cyanotic phenotype with a consistent crying trigger makes a primary arrhythmia a remote possibility. (Source: RCH CPG: Breath holding spells)

explanation.summary: Breath-holding spells affect up to 5 per cent of young children and divide into a cyanotic type, provoked by anger or frustration, and a pallid type, provoked by pain or fright and mediated by vagal asystole. The diagnosis rests on the stereotyped sequence of provocation, cry, colour change and brief loss of tone with rapid recovery, and investigations are directed at the two things that genuinely change management: iron deficiency and, in atypical or pallid cases, a cardiac conduction abnormality. Iron deficiency is present in a large proportion of affected children and correcting it reduces spell frequency, which is the only pharmacological intervention with a reasonable evidence base. Parents are taught to lay the child flat on their side and let the event end on its own, avoiding shaking, mouth-to-mouth or cold water. The condition resolves spontaneously by school age and does not increase the risk of epilepsy.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical: a provocation, a prolonged cry, then colour change and loss of tone with rapid recovery
Check a full blood count and ferritin in every child with breath-holding spells
Iron replacement reduces spell frequency and is the only drug treatment with useful evidence
Reserve electroencephalography for events without a trigger, during sleep, or with prolonged recovery
Consider an electrocardiogram for pallid spells or a family history of sudden death
explanation.pearls: Cow milk intake above 500 mL per day in a toddler is itself a cause of iron deficiency through occult gut blood loss and calcium mediated inhibition of iron absorption; capping milk at 500 mL is part of the treatment, not an afterthought.

subtopic_detail: Threshold for specialist assessment of an asymptomatic murmur first heard in early infancy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar performing a 6-week health check on a 5-week-old girl. Her mother has no concerns and says she feeds for about twenty minutes on each side without stopping to rest, and has never gone sweaty or dusky during a feed.

She was born at 38 weeks by elective caesarean section for breech presentation. Birth weight was 3200 g and she now weighs 4100 g. Her newborn examination at 12 hours of age was documented as normal with no murmur heard.

On examination she is pink and alert. There is a grade 2/6 systolic murmur heard at the left sternal edge with no radiation and no thrill. Heart sounds are normal with a single second sound. Femoral pulses are equal in volume to the brachial pulses. Pre-ductal and post-ductal oxygen saturations are both 99 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99 per cent pre-ductal and post-ductal, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Cardiovascular examination: Grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, no thrill, no radiation, normal single second heart sound
data_table.Pulses: Femoral pulses equal in volume to brachial pulses
data_table.Growth: Birth weight 3200 g, current weight 4100 g, tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the murmur at the twelve month health check
options.rationale: The features that allow a murmur to be called innocent at the bedside, such as a vibratory Still murmur that softens on standing, are not reliably assessable in early infancy. A murmur appearing after a documented normal newborn examination is exactly the pattern seen when a ventricular septal defect becomes audible as pulmonary vascular resistance falls. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph and an electrocardiogram before deciding on referral
options.rationale: Chest radiography and electrocardiography are insensitive for the defects that present this way and a normal pair of tests does not exclude a significant lesion. Echocardiography has superseded both as the investigation that settles the question. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Measure four limb blood pressures and reassure the parents if the readings are equal
options.rationale: Four limb pressures screen for coarctation, and the equal volume femoral pulses already make that diagnosis unlikely, so a normal result would not explain the murmur. Excluding one lesion is not the same as characterising the murmur. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Review her in the practice in three months and refer only if the murmur persists
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate for an asymptomatic murmur with clearly innocent characteristics in an older child, not for a new murmur under 1 year of age. A left-to-right shunt can drive heart failure and faltering growth well within a three month window. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

options.text: Refer for paediatric cardiology review with echocardiography within the next few weeks
options.rationale: Any murmur first detected under 1 year of age warrants specialist assessment with echocardiography, because a substantial proportion represent structural disease and bedside criteria for innocence do not perform well at this age. She is well and growing, so the referral is timely rather than emergency, and the family can be told that many such murmurs prove to be small defects or normal flow. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart murmurs)

explanation.summary: Murmurs are heard in a large minority of children at some point, and most are innocent, but the prior probability of structural disease is far higher in the first year of life than later in childhood. The newborn examination misses lesions whose murmur depends on a pressure gradient that only develops as pulmonary vascular resistance falls over the first weeks, so a ventricular septal defect or an atrioventricular septal defect commonly declares itself at the 6 week check rather than at birth. Features that would prompt urgent rather than routine referral include poor feeding with sweating or tachypnoea, faltering growth, a diastolic murmur, a thrill, absent or delayed femoral pulses, cyanosis or an abnormal second heart sound. Echocardiography is the investigation of choice; chest radiography and electrocardiography lack the sensitivity to exclude significant disease. In an older child with a classic Still murmur, normal pulses and no symptoms, reassurance without imaging is entirely reasonable.
key_points: A murmur first heard under 1 year of age warrants specialist assessment with echocardiography
A normal newborn check does not exclude a shunt lesion that becomes audible weeks later
Chest radiography and electrocardiography are not sensitive enough to exclude structural disease
Red flags for urgent referral include feeding difficulty, faltering growth, diastolic murmur, thrill, weak femoral pulses or cyanosis
Bedside criteria for an innocent murmur are reliable in older children, not in infants
explanation.pearls: A ventricular septal defect murmur is loudest when the defect is small: as the defect gets larger the gradient falls, so a quiet murmur with a loud pulmonary second sound and tachypnoea is more worrying than a loud isolated murmur.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of paediatric heart murmurs
